mainEntity.name: Is it normal for a toothache to come and go?

acceptedAnswer.text: Intermittent tooth pain can occur for a number of reasons. Early-stage decay, mild gum inflammation, or temporary sensitivity from enamel erosion may cause discomfort that seems to appear and disappear. However, pain that keeps returning — even if it is not constant — may indicate an underlying issue that could progress over time. It is generally advisable to mention recurring symptoms to your dentist at your next appointment, or sooner if the pain becomes more frequent or intense, so that the cause can be investigated properly.

mainEntity.name: Can teeth grinding cause pain only at night?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, bruxism-related pain is often most noticeable at night or upon waking because the grinding and clenching typically occur during sleep. You may not be aware of the habit at all. Over time, bruxism can lead to tooth sensitivity, jaw stiffness, headaches, and worn tooth surfaces. Your dentist can assess for signs of bruxism during an examination and may recommend a custom night guard to help protect your teeth and reduce discomfort. Addressing contributing factors such as stress may also be beneficial.

mainEntity.name: Should I go to A&E for a toothache at night?

acceptedAnswer.text: A&E departments are generally not equipped to provide dental treatment. However, if you experience significant facial swelling that affects your ability to breathe or swallow, or if you develop a high fever alongside dental pain, seeking urgent medical attention is appropriate. For non-emergency dental pain at night, using temporary home measures until you can contact your dental practice during working hours is usually the most practical approach. Many practices offer same-day or urgent appointment slots for patients experiencing acute discomfort.

mainEntity.name: Can a sinus infection feel like a toothache?

acceptedAnswer.text: Absolutely. The roots of the upper back teeth (premolars and molars) sit very close to the maxillary sinuses. When these sinuses become inflamed or congested — due to a cold, allergies, or infection — the resulting pressure can create a sensation that closely mimics toothache. This type of discomfort often affects multiple upper teeth rather than a single tooth and may be accompanied by nasal congestion, facial pressure, or a feeling of fullness. Your dentist can help distinguish between sinus-related discomfort and a dental issue during a clinical examination.

mainEntity.name: How can I tell if my nighttime toothache is serious?

acceptedAnswer.text: While any dental discomfort is worth monitoring, certain signs may suggest that prompt professional assessment is advisable. These include pain that is severe or progressively worsening, swelling in the gum or face, sensitivity to temperature that persists after the stimulus is removed, pain when biting, or any sign of discharge near a tooth. A throbbing pain that keeps you awake on multiple nights is also worth investigating. Your dentist can carry out appropriate tests — including visual examination, X-rays, and sensitivity assessments — to determine the cause and discuss suitable options.

mainEntity.name: Does nighttime toothache always mean I need a root canal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. Nighttime toothache can result from many different causes, and not all of them require root canal treatment. Mild sensitivity, early decay, gum inflammation, bruxism, and sinus issues can all cause nighttime dental discomfort and may be managed with other approaches. Root canal treatment is typically considered when the dental pulp inside a tooth has become irreversibly inflamed or infected. Only a thorough clinical examination can determine the cause of your symptoms and the most appropriate course of action for your individual situation.
